children: As GROHE SPA brings its premium showering collection to Delhi airport, LIXIL IMEA’s Priya Rustogi explains how experiential marketing can build brand consideration before consumers enter the purchase cycle and why footfall alone is not a measure of ROI

GROHE SPA’s three-month installation at Delhi International Airport tests the potential of experiential marketing to reach consumers outside conventional retail. For Priya Rustogi of LIXIL IMEA, the opportunity lies not merely in visibility, but in building brand familiarity and consideration long before a purchase decision.

Airports have long offered brands access to large, diverse audiences. But high footfall does not necessarily translate into consumer intent, and visibility alone offers limited insight into whether an advertising investment will influence a purchase. For marketers, the challenge is to turn a fleeting encounter into something that remains relevant after the consumer leaves the terminal.

GROHE SPA, the premium luxury showering collection from GROHE, is exploring that opportunity through an installation at Terminal 3 of Delhi International Airport. Running from October to December 2026, the display brings the brand’s design and technology into a high-footfall public space, taking product discovery beyond the traditional showroom.

Described by the company as a world first for GROHE SPA, the installation centres on an immersive Aqua Sanctuary inspired by water, design and wellbeing. Its premise is to introduce travellers to premium bathroom design in a setting where they may not be actively looking for it.

For Priya Rustogi, Leader (Managing Director), India, LIXIL IMEA, the initiative reflects a broader shift in how premium brands can approach consumer engagement. The objective is not simply to attract attention, but to influence how people perceive and remember a brand before they enter an active purchase cycle.

“For a premium category such as bathrooms, marketing effectiveness cannot be measured by footfall alone. The more important question is whether an experience helps people understand the brand differently, creates interest in the category and influences consideration over time. This is particularly relevant for GROHE SPA, given that purchase decisions involve considerable research, planning and deliberation,” Rustogi says.

That distinction defines the marketing challenge. An airport installation can generate exposure, but its value depends on whether the experience communicates the brand’s proposition and creates an association that survives beyond the immediate encounter.
Reaching Consumers Before They Enter The Purchase Cycle

Bathroom fittings are not typically impulse purchases. Decisions can involve home design, renovation plans, product research, budgets and consultations with architects or designers. By the time consumers visit a showroom, they may already have formed preferences about the brands and products they want to explore.
GROHE’s airport installation seeks to engage consumers earlier, when a specific purchase need may not yet exist.

Rustogi says the choice of an airport is intended to take the brand beyond conventional points of product discovery. Consumers usually encounter bathroom solutions while building a home, renovating or actively researching products. An airport offers an opportunity to introduce the brand before that process begins.

“The choice of an airport is based on the opportunity to introduce GROHE SPA in a setting beyond conventional points of product discovery. Consumers typically encounter bathroom solutions when they are already renovating, building a home or actively exploring products. An airport offers a different context, allowing us to reach an audience that may not currently be in the market but could consider a premium bathroom upgrade in the future. This enables us to create an impression before a specific purchase need arises,” she says.

The strategy is built around the possibility that brand preference begins forming before a consumer starts shopping. In this context, the airport becomes a platform for introducing the brand rather than necessarily generating an immediate transaction.

The physical nature of the installation also matters. Premium bathroom solutions are evaluated on more than functionality: aesthetics, material quality, finish and the overall experience contribute to perceptions of value. A physical display can bring those elements into a setting where consumers would not ordinarily expect to encounter them.

Rustogi explains that the installation is intended to make the product experience more tangible than a catalogue, showroom visit or digital image, allowing travellers to engage with GROHE SPA’s design and finish.

“The objective is to create a memorable brand encounter that builds familiarity and aspiration, giving consumers a reason to explore GROHE when a relevant need emerges. In high-consideration categories such as bathrooms, preference often begins forming well before the purchase decision. By engaging consumers at this earlier stage, we aim to make GROHE SPA a part of their consideration set when they eventually plan a bathroom upgrade,” she says.

The distinction is important for measuring success. The installation may reach people who have no immediate plans to renovate, but the brand’s intended benefit is longer-term consideration. Whether the experience actually changes future purchase behaviour, however, will need to be established through measurement rather than assumed from exposure.
From Visibility To Measurable Consumer Interest
For marketers, the challenge with high-footfall environments is separating the number of people who pass an installation from those who notice it, engage with it and remember the brand.

For a premium category with a potentially long purchase cycle, conventional reach and impression figures are only part of the picture. A traveller may stop to look at the installation without having an immediate need. Another may already be researching a bathroom upgrade and be closer to a decision. Both contribute to the audience, but their relationship with the brand is different.
Rustogi says GROHE would assess the installation using a combination of visibility, audience engagement, brand recall and observable interest across its consumer touchpoints.

“We would evaluate the installation through multiple parameters, including visibility, the quality of audience engagement, brand recall and any observable increase in interest across our consumer touchpoints. Website traffic, showroom enquiries and qualified leads would provide a more tangible view of its contribution to the consumer journey,” she says.

Her response points towards a measurement framework that combines the immediate experience with downstream indicators. Website visits and showroom enquiries could help identify whether the installation encourages further exploration, while qualified leads may provide a closer connection to potential commercial outcomes.

However, these are evaluation parameters outlined by Rustogi, not disclosed campaign targets. The material provided does not specify numerical benchmarks, attribution methods or confirmed results from the activation.

The distinction matters because an enquiry or sale occurring after an airport encounter does not necessarily mean the installation caused it. Consumers may have encountered the brand through other marketing channels, and several influences can contribute to a high-value purchase.
Rustogi acknowledges this limitation, noting that eventual sales must be assessed in the context of the time between initial exposure and purchase, as well as other factors shaping the decision.

“Eventual sales, however, need to be assessed with the understanding that a purchase may happen well after the initial interaction and involve several other influences. For a high-involvement category such as bathrooms, the impact of experiential marketing also lies in building familiarity and strengthening brand consideration before consumers enter an active purchase cycle,” she says.

For GROHE SPA, the intended outcome is therefore not limited to immediate conversion. The more fundamental question is whether the experience makes the brand more memorable and increases the likelihood of it being considered when a consumer eventually plans a bathroom upgrade.
Can A One-off Installation Become A Repeatable Channel?

A distinctive installation can generate attention, but its value as a marketing channel depends on more than the novelty of the format. Brands must determine whether the environment reaches a relevant audience, whether the experience communicates the product’s value and whether the resulting engagement justifies the investment.
For Rustogi, the decision to repeat an airport-based experience would depend on several considerations rather than footfall alone.

“A first-of-its-kind installation can generate attention, but its long-term value depends on whether it reaches the right audiences, communicates the brand proposition effectively and contributes to stronger consideration. When deciding a marketing channel several considerations need to be made like quality of engagement, investment required, visibility achieved and any measurable influence on consumer interactions,” she says.
This raises a broader question for experiential marketing: can a format designed around one brand and one location be scaled without losing its relevance?

Rustogi believes the approach could extend to other high-consideration home categories where design, craftsmanship and product experience influence purchase decisions. But she cautions against treating the airport model as a format that can simply be replicated everywhere.

“Similarly, feasibility as a recurring model depends on whether the airport environment genuinely fits the products on display. High footfall alone does not guarantee effectiveness; the format must engage relevant audiences, communicate the product’s value and complement other touchpoints across the purchase journey. This approach could extend to other high-consideration home categories where design, craftsmanship and product experience influence purchase decisions. However, success would depend on identifying environments that are relevant to both the product and its intended audience, rather than replicating the same format across locations,” she says.

The argument moves the discussion away from the novelty of the installation towards its strategic role. An airport experience may suit a premium product whose value can be communicated through design and physical presence, but the same approach may not be equally effective for every category or audience.

For marketers considering similar activations, the central question is whether the experience complements the wider consumer journey. It must offer something beyond the visibility available through conventional media while creating a plausible route towards further engagement.
The Real ROI Lies Beyond The Airport

GROHE SPA’s three-month installation reflects an effort to bring premium product discovery into an environment outside conventional retail. It also illustrates the distinction between creating a memorable brand experience and demonstrating measurable commercial returns.

For high-consideration categories, experiential marketing can help introduce a brand before an active purchase need emerges. But its contribution must be assessed through more than the number of people who pass the display. Brand recall, the quality of engagement, subsequent product exploration and qualified enquiries can all help build a more complete picture, although attributing eventual sales requires careful consideration of other influences.
Rustogi sees experiential marketing as one part of a broader consumer engagement strategy.

“Ultimately, experiential marketing will be part of a broader consumer engagement strategy, using physical interactions to strengthen brand associations and build consideration that can influence future purchase decisions,” she says.

That is the distinction at the heart of the airport attention economy. Footfall can create an opportunity to be seen, but it does not establish intent or guarantee a return. For a brand such as GROHE SPA, the commercial test is whether the encounter stays with the consumer long enough to influence a future decision—and whether the brand can gather credible evidence of that influence.

The installation provides an opportunity to explore that proposition. Whether it becomes a repeatable marketing channel will depend not simply on how many travellers encounter it, but on what the brand can demonstrate about engagement, consideration and the value generated beyond the terminal.
